# ~/DEV Knowledge Graph Refresh (185 → 2,190 Files)

On 2026-09-01 the stale April graphify build of `~/DEV` (185 files) was rebuilt against the current 2,190-file corpus, with Codex running independent verification passes over the artifact. The session finalized at 9,256 nodes, 18,341 edges, and 628 named communities at `~/DEV/graphify-out/graph.html`, with zero correctness defects and zero regressions per Codex, but with completeness deliberately left incomplete: 1,099 files and 95 of 130 converted office documents remain unextracted, blocked by the Gemini free-tier daily quota. Resume instructions live in `~/DEV/graphify-out/RESUME.md`.

## Key Points

- **Chunk size drives extraction yield nonlinearly:** 60 files per chunk yielded 17%, 20 files yielded ~38%, and 15 files yielded 100%. `GF_CHUNK=15` is the settled value; the resume command is `GF_CHUNK=15 ~/DEV/graphify-out/scripts/office_loop.sh 25 6`.
- **Gemini free tier enforces two independent caps** — 5 requests/minute *and* 20/day per model. The per-minute cap is the operative bottleneck because each request burns roughly 5 minutes in backoff; the daily cap was confirmed *not* to reset at midnight during a post-midnight retry.
- **Rebuild the graph after every extraction pass.** A graph built at 20:55 was shipped alongside a Gemini extraction layer written at 01:22, so 0 of 256 Gemini nodes appeared in the artifact. The merge code was correct — it had simply never been re-run against the newer layer.
- **Five real defects found across the passes:** the missing graph layer above; a scope filter silently dropping all 130 office docs (they convert to `.md` *inside* an excluded folder); one minified vendor file producing 650 junk nodes and 3,699 junk edges; zero-yield files marked "done" so they would never retry (221 requeued); and an omitted `root=` argument collapsing paths to basenames and zeroing attribution.
- **Long-running extraction must checkpoint.** Save-at-the-end meant a 10-minute foreground timeout wiped an entire pass; checkpointing now happens every 30 files. Background jobs were separately killed externally twice — background execution is not a safety guarantee for long jobs.

## Details

The dominant technical finding is the chunk-size/yield relationship, which is steep enough to change the shape of the job rather than just its speed. Moving from 60 to 15 files per chunk took extraction yield from 17% to 100%, meaning larger chunks were not merely slower but were silently discarding the majority of their input. Combined with the Gemini free tier's 5-requests-per-minute ceiling — which converts each request into roughly five minutes of wall-clock backoff — the extraction leg is fundamentally a slow, quota-metered pipeline whose throughput cannot be improved by batching harder. That constraint is what forced the session's central decision: after three consecutive failures (two external background-job kills and a foreground rate-limit wall), work stopped and the graph was finalized with the state on hand rather than burning further attempts against a quota that a post-midnight retry proved had not reset.

The stale-layer bug is the most instructive of the five defects because nothing in the pipeline reported an error. The graph artifact was built before its own newest input existed, so a correct merge implementation produced an artifact missing 256 nodes while every component reported success. This is the same shape as the manifest-omission class in [[concepts/backup-manifest-drift-and-launchd-status-lag]]: the executed steps all succeeded, and the defect lives entirely in what was never included. The scope filter dropping all 130 office docs has the same character — the conversion step wrote `.md` outputs into a folder the extractor excluded, so a hundred-plus documents disappeared between two individually-correct stages. The operational rule the session settled on, "rebuild the graph and re-export HTML after every extraction pass, then re-run Codex verification before calling it done," exists precisely because per-stage success does not compose into artifact correctness.

Two process lessons carry beyond graphify. First, scripts living in the job scratch folder die with the job — a trap already flagged in the user's own notes and repeated here; all 15 scripts were relocated to `~/DEV/graphify-out/scripts/` and shell wrappers repointed, since the wrappers still held stale scratch paths. The Codex verification reports were likewise copied out of the disposable scratch folder into `~/DEV/graphify-out/` so the handoff document would reference durable paths. Second, when the user caught a logging bug that printed `0 nodes` while nodes actually existed, the discrepancy was explained away rather than fixed — recorded as an explicit instruction to push to fix rather than rationalize. A handoff document was written for resumption in another session, secret-scanned clean with all referenced paths verified, though it was placed in a `/var/folders/.../T/` temp path. Two open ARMS gaps noted in that handoff remain unaddressed.

# Connection: Verify Directly, Don't Trust the Intermediate Layer

## The Connection

Both substantive sessions on 2026-04-22 ran into a version of the same problem: a tool or agent produced output that *looked* fine - a citation with a plausible author list, a photo wired into HTML with a correct relative path - but was actually wrong or unverifiable through the usual checking method. In [[concepts/sportscience-research-repo-batch-import]], a background repair agent's citation fixes for IDs 286, 287, and 358 contained hallucinated author lists despite correctly identifying the papers' topics. In [[concepts/the-monitor-newsletter]], Blake Wright's photo failed to appear in the localhost preview server even though the HTML and file path were both correct.

## Key Insight

In both cases, the fix was not to redo the original work but to change the *verification method* to something closer to the ground truth. The hallucinated citations were caught by extracting the actual PDF text with PyPDF2 and reading it directly, rather than trusting the agent's summarized output. The "broken" photo was confirmed to be fine by opening the HTML file directly in Chrome via `file://`, rather than trusting the brainstorm preview server's rendering. The shared lesson: when an agent, tool, or service produces output that looks plausible but can't be easily double-checked through the same channel, step down to a more primitive, lower-level check (raw file text, direct file rendering) before accepting the result as correct.

## Evidence

- 2026-04-22 (10:57): "Background agent produced `docs/batch_r7_fixes.json` but hallucinated wrong author lists for IDs 286, 287, and 358... Used PyPDF2 text extraction to verify actual authors and corrected all three citations before committing."
- 2026-04-22 (17:21): "Photo failed to render in localhost preview — identified as a server limitation (brainstorm preview server doesn't serve image files), not an HTML error... always verify photo rendering by opening the HTML directly in Chrome via file:// URL."

# Stack Doctor Sweep (2026-08-11): Self-Inflicted Repo Divergence and a Lying Dry Run

A `/claude-stack-doctor` run on 2026-08-11 after a three-day gap took the automation/memory stack from 8 issues to 6 (three of the remaining six being lagging indicators that clear on the next nightly backup). The sweep's most valuable findings were not the fixes themselves but three cases where the *monitoring layer* was the defect: a nightly backup that committed its own generated files and so diverged a repo every night, a `skill-tax` check measuring the wrong quantity, and a `-DryRun` flag that reported git operations it never performed.

## Key Points

- **`repo-diverged:skills` was self-inflicted.** Six tracked files were regenerated every run (`last-weekly-run.log` plus five `__pycache__` entries), so the nightly backup committed churn and diverged the repo nightly. Untracking and gitignoring them was the sweep's highest-leverage fix.
- **`daily-backup.ps1 -DryRun` was lying.** The `Log` calls at lines 28/38 sat *outside* the `if (-not $DryRun)` guards at 24/34, so a dry run printed "committed / pushed" for git operations it never ran — briefly fooling the sweep itself. Fixed to `[dry-run] would commit`.
- **`skill-tax` was a false positive from the monitor's own logic:** it counted all 133 on-disk `SKILL.md` files with no knowledge of `skillOverrides`. Verified empirically first (0 of 72 overridden skills leak into the listing; 61 expected, 60 seen), *then* the script was patched — the two candidate fixes were opposite, so the discriminating check had to precede either.
- **`flush-error` recurrence across 8/08 and 8/11 indicated version skew, not contention:** `claude-agent-sdk` was 26 versions behind (0.2.110 → 0.2.136); upgrading restored flushes, and the memsearch flush patch was confirmed to survive the package operation.
- **Both sides preserved on a two-writer conflict.** Four SecondBrain morning briefings differed from committed origin versions; origin's won by default and are live, with local copies staged at `doctor-backup-20260807-135924/secondbrain-local-briefings/*.local.md` — fully reversible rather than adjudicated on the spot.

## Details

The three monitoring-layer defects share a structure worth naming: each produced a confident, well-formatted signal about a system state it was not actually measuring. The dry-run bug is the purest form — logging placed outside the guard it describes means the flag's entire purpose (previewing without acting) is silently void, and the operator's trust in the preview is inversely related to its accuracy. `skill-tax` is the same failure one level up: the check counted files on disk, a proxy that was correct before `skillOverrides` existed and became wrong afterward, so a previously-completed cleanup appeared not to have landed. The correct response in that case was explicitly *not* to fix either candidate immediately, because the two possible remedies (clean up more skills, or patch the counter) pointed in opposite directions; running the discriminating check first — do overridden skills leak into the listing? — decided which. The `repo-diverged:skills` case is the automation eating its own output: a backup job that commits generated artifacts guarantees divergence on every run, making a real alarm fire nightly for a cause the alarm cannot describe.

The sweep's restraint is as instructive as its fixes. Several issues were deliberately left alone with reasons recorded: 73 unversioned skill files (a design fork — adding `~/.agents/skills` to `backup-manifest.json` was proposed but not applied), unmanaged `DEV` directories (the user's scope call), a 4-log compiler backlog (self-healing at 2/night against ~1/day, and forcing it costs real money), and `snapshot:sessions` (an rsync race against a live Codex file, not rot). Two items were escalated as genuinely not auto-fixable and left open: Outlook auth expired, so morning briefings were shipping with 0 email threads pending an interactive `reauth.sh` run, and Google Drive 154h stale, with files reaching the local `G:` cache but GoogleDriveFS not syncing. The `MEMORY.md` file was at 100% — the next write would have failed — and was consolidated to 93% by shortening wording while keeping all 16 threads, rather than dropping any. Finally, two `flush-error` session IDs were classified benign only after evidence (the IDs exist nowhere; the DEV slug holds 28 transcripts, 3 in the last 24h), on the explicit principle of not classifying by inference; and two self-corrections were made before reporting (an "8 → 2" claim against a raw verdict of 6, and a claim that the /doctor changes were unversioned when the nightly backup had in fact committed them).

# Pre-Registration as a Substitute for an Absent External Reviewer

When an analysis has no second reader, the usual defense against post-hoc threshold tuning — someone else checking the reasoning — is unavailable. The S2_Evaluation session on 2026-08-08 surfaced this explicitly (Q25: "who is the sports science reviewer?" — the user confirmed it was himself) and answered it structurally: commit the thresholds and decision records to version control **before the data exists**, so the pre-registration carries a verifiable timestamp instead of an assertion.

## Key Points

- **Asking "who reviews this?" is a design question, not an administrative one.** The answer changes which safeguards are load-bearing; a design that assumes a reviewer and does not have one is unguarded in a way nobody notices.
- **A timestamp in git is falsifiable; a claim in a document is not.** Nine ADRs were committed at 22:46:32, before the CSV export existed, making "these thresholds were fixed in advance" checkable by a third party rather than taken on trust.
- **Pre-commitment must include the negative outcome.** S2 pre-declared that a negative gate result — no athlete clears the 1.5-SD threshold — is still written up and published. Without that rule, a threshold silently becomes a filter for interesting-looking output.
- **Absolute thresholds pre-commit; relative ones do not.** "≥1.5 population SD" can return zero names; "top 3 by deviation" always returns three, so it encodes no prior claim about what counts as unusual and cannot be violated by the data.
- **Record decisions only where trade-offs are real.** ADRs were written for consequential choices and deliberately omitted for cheap-to-reverse presentation questions, keeping the decision log a signal rather than a transcript.

## Details

The mechanism this defends against is not dishonesty but ordinary drift. An analyst who sets a threshold after seeing the data cannot fully separate "this cut point is principled" from "this cut point produces a plausible-looking list of names," and no amount of good faith resolves the ambiguity from the inside. External review normally breaks the loop by introducing a reader who did not see the intermediate results. When that reader does not exist, the loop must be broken temporally instead: the decision is fixed at a point where the data could not have influenced it, and that point is made externally verifiable. Git supplies exactly this — an authenticated ordering of commits that a skeptic can inspect without trusting the author's account of when they decided what.

The distinction between absolute and relative thresholds is what makes the pre-registration bite. A relative rule ("flag the top 3") is unfalsifiable by construction: whatever the data look like, it produces the same quantity of output, so committing to it in advance commits to nothing. An absolute rule ("flag anyone past 1.5 population SD") encodes a substantive prior claim about what magnitude is worth a coach's attention, and it can be wrong — it can return nobody. That possibility is the whole point, which is why the companion rule (publish the negative result) is not an afterthought. A threshold that is only reported when it fires has been quietly converted back into a selection procedure. The same logic explains why the room-size floor came with a *renamed* fallback rather than a silent one: changing the comparison population changes what the number means, so the artifact's claim has to change with it.

The practice generalizes beyond statistics to any output whose quality cannot be checked from the output alone. The recurring theme across this knowledge base — verify at ground truth rather than trusting the layer above — usually applies downstream, to results. Pre-registration is the upstream form: when downstream verification is impossible because there is no independent channel to verify against, move the check earlier, to a point where the reasoning can still be pinned down and time-stamped. The cost is small and front-loaded; the alternative is an analysis whose thresholds are, in principle, unauditable. A related discipline is to keep the record proportional: writing an ADR for every choice dilutes the log until the consequential commitments are indistinguishable from formatting preferences, so only decisions with genuine trade-offs earn a record.

# ~/DEV Knowledge Graph Refresh (185 → 2,190 Files)

On 2026-09-01 the stale April graphify build of `~/DEV` (185 files) was rebuilt against the current 2,190-file corpus, with Codex running independent verification passes over the artifact. The session finalized at 9,256 nodes, 18,341 edges, and 628 named communities at `~/DEV/graphify-out/graph.html`, with zero correctness defects and zero regressions per Codex, but with completeness deliberately left incomplete: 1,099 files and 95 of 130 converted office documents remain unextracted, blocked by the Gemini free-tier daily quota. Resume instructions live in `~/DEV/graphify-out/RESUME.md`.

## Key Points

- **Chunk size drives extraction yield nonlinearly:** 60 files per chunk yielded 17%, 20 files yielded ~38%, and 15 files yielded 100%. `GF_CHUNK=15` is the settled value; the resume command is `GF_CHUNK=15 ~/DEV/graphify-out/scripts/office_loop.sh 25 6`.
- **Gemini free tier enforces two independent caps** — 5 requests/minute *and* 20/day per model. The per-minute cap is the operative bottleneck because each request burns roughly 5 minutes in backoff; the daily cap was confirmed *not* to reset at midnight during a post-midnight retry.
- **Rebuild the graph after every extraction pass.** A graph built at 20:55 was shipped alongside a Gemini extraction layer written at 01:22, so 0 of 256 Gemini nodes appeared in the artifact. The merge code was correct — it had simply never been re-run against the newer layer.
- **Five real defects found across the passes:** the missing graph layer above; a scope filter silently dropping all 130 office docs (they convert to `.md` *inside* an excluded folder); one minified vendor file producing 650 junk nodes and 3,699 junk edges; zero-yield files marked "done" so they would never retry (221 requeued); and an omitted `root=` argument collapsing paths to basenames and zeroing attribution.
- **Long-running extraction must checkpoint.** Save-at-the-end meant a 10-minute foreground timeout wiped an entire pass; checkpointing now happens every 30 files. Background jobs were separately killed externally twice — background execution is not a safety guarantee for long jobs.

## Details

The dominant technical finding is the chunk-size/yield relationship, which is steep enough to change the shape of the job rather than just its speed. Moving from 60 to 15 files per chunk took extraction yield from 17% to 100%, meaning larger chunks were not merely slower but were silently discarding the majority of their input. Combined with the Gemini free tier's 5-requests-per-minute ceiling — which converts each request into roughly five minutes of wall-clock backoff — the extraction leg is fundamentally a slow, quota-metered pipeline whose throughput cannot be improved by batching harder. That constraint is what forced the session's central decision: after three consecutive failures (two external background-job kills and a foreground rate-limit wall), work stopped and the graph was finalized with the state on hand rather than burning further attempts against a quota that a post-midnight retry proved had not reset.

The stale-layer bug is the most instructive of the five defects because nothing in the pipeline reported an error. The graph artifact was built before its own newest input existed, so a correct merge implementation produced an artifact missing 256 nodes while every component reported success. This is the same shape as the manifest-omission class in [[concepts/backup-manifest-drift-and-launchd-status-lag]]: the executed steps all succeeded, and the defect lives entirely in what was never included. The scope filter dropping all 130 office docs has the same character — the conversion step wrote `.md` outputs into a folder the extractor excluded, so a hundred-plus documents disappeared between two individually-correct stages. The operational rule the session settled on, "rebuild the graph and re-export HTML after every extraction pass, then re-run Codex verification before calling it done," exists precisely because per-stage success does not compose into artifact correctness.

Two process lessons carry beyond graphify. First, scripts living in the job scratch folder die with the job — a trap already flagged in the user's own notes and repeated here; all 15 scripts were relocated to `~/DEV/graphify-out/scripts/` and shell wrappers repointed, since the wrappers still held stale scratch paths. The Codex verification reports were likewise copied out of the disposable scratch folder into `~/DEV/graphify-out/` so the handoff document would reference durable paths. Second, when the user caught a logging bug that printed `0 nodes` while nodes actually existed, the discrepancy was explained away rather than fixed — recorded as an explicit instruction to push to fix rather than rationalize. A handoff document was written for resumption in another session, secret-scanned clean with all referenced paths verified, though it was placed in a `/var/folders/.../T/` temp path. Two open ARMS gaps noted in that handoff remain unaddressed.

# Connection: Verify Directly, Don't Trust the Intermediate Layer

## The Connection

Both substantive sessions on 2026-04-22 ran into a version of the same problem: a tool or agent produced output that *looked* fine - a citation with a plausible author list, a photo wired into HTML with a correct relative path - but was actually wrong or unverifiable through the usual checking method. In [[concepts/sportscience-research-repo-batch-import]], a background repair agent's citation fixes for IDs 286, 287, and 358 contained hallucinated author lists despite correctly identifying the papers' topics. In [[concepts/the-monitor-newsletter]], Blake Wright's photo failed to appear in the localhost preview server even though the HTML and file path were both correct.

## Key Insight

In both cases, the fix was not to redo the original work but to change the *verification method* to something closer to the ground truth. The hallucinated citations were caught by extracting the actual PDF text with PyPDF2 and reading it directly, rather than trusting the agent's summarized output. The "broken" photo was confirmed to be fine by opening the HTML file directly in Chrome via `file://`, rather than trusting the brainstorm preview server's rendering. The shared lesson: when an agent, tool, or service produces output that looks plausible but can't be easily double-checked through the same channel, step down to a more primitive, lower-level check (raw file text, direct file rendering) before accepting the result as correct.

# Stack Doctor Sweep (2026-08-11): Self-Inflicted Repo Divergence and a Lying Dry Run

A `/claude-stack-doctor` run on 2026-08-11 after a three-day gap took the automation/memory stack from 8 issues to 6 (three of the remaining six being lagging indicators that clear on the next nightly backup). The sweep's most valuable findings were not the fixes themselves but three cases where the *monitoring layer* was the defect: a nightly backup that committed its own generated files and so diverged a repo every night, a `skill-tax` check measuring the wrong quantity, and a `-DryRun` flag that reported git operations it never performed.

## Key Points

- **`repo-diverged:skills` was self-inflicted.** Six tracked files were regenerated every run (`last-weekly-run.log` plus five `__pycache__` entries), so the nightly backup committed churn and diverged the repo nightly. Untracking and gitignoring them was the sweep's highest-leverage fix.
- **`daily-backup.ps1 -DryRun` was lying.** The `Log` calls at lines 28/38 sat *outside* the `if (-not $DryRun)` guards at 24/34, so a dry run printed "committed / pushed" for git operations it never ran — briefly fooling the sweep itself. Fixed to `[dry-run] would commit`.
- **`skill-tax` was a false positive from the monitor's own logic:** it counted all 133 on-disk `SKILL.md` files with no knowledge of `skillOverrides`. Verified empirically first (0 of 72 overridden skills leak into the listing; 61 expected, 60 seen), *then* the script was patched — the two candidate fixes were opposite, so the discriminating check had to precede either.
- **`flush-error` recurrence across 8/08 and 8/11 indicated version skew, not contention:** `claude-agent-sdk` was 26 versions behind (0.2.110 → 0.2.136); upgrading restored flushes, and the memsearch flush patch was confirmed to survive the package operation.
- **Both sides preserved on a two-writer conflict.** Four SecondBrain morning briefings differed from committed origin versions; origin's won by default and are live, with local copies staged at `doctor-backup-20260807-135924/secondbrain-local-briefings/*.local.md` — fully reversible rather than adjudicated on the spot.

## Details

The three monitoring-layer defects share a structure worth naming: each produced a confident, well-formatted signal about a system state it was not actually measuring. The dry-run bug is the purest form — logging placed outside the guard it describes means the flag's entire purpose (previewing without acting) is silently void, and the operator's trust in the preview is inversely related to its accuracy. `skill-tax` is the same failure one level up: the check counted files on disk, a proxy that was correct before `skillOverrides` existed and became wrong afterward, so a previously-completed cleanup appeared not to have landed. The correct response in that case was explicitly *not* to fix either candidate immediately, because the two possible remedies (clean up more skills, or patch the counter) pointed in opposite directions; running the discriminating check first — do overridden skills leak into the listing? — decided which. The `repo-diverged:skills` case is the automation eating its own output: a backup job that commits generated artifacts guarantees divergence on every run, making a real alarm fire nightly for a cause the alarm cannot describe.

The sweep's restraint is as instructive as its fixes. Several issues were deliberately left alone with reasons recorded: 73 unversioned skill files (a design fork — adding `~/.agents/skills` to `backup-manifest.json` was proposed but not applied), unmanaged `DEV` directories (the user's scope call), a 4-log compiler backlog (self-healing at 2/night against ~1/day, and forcing it costs real money), and `snapshot:sessions` (an rsync race against a live Codex file, not rot). The `MEMORY.md` file was at 100% — the next write would have failed — and was consolidated to 93% by shortening wording while keeping all 16 threads, rather than dropping any. Finally, two `flush-error` session IDs were classified benign only after evidence (the IDs exist nowhere; the DEV slug holds 28 transcripts, 3 in the last 24h), on the explicit principle of not classifying by inference; and two self-corrections were made before reporting (an "8 → 2" claim against a raw verdict of 6, and a claim that the /doctor changes were unversioned when the nightly backup had in fact committed them).

# Pre-Registration as a Substitute for an Absent External Reviewer

When an analysis has no second reader, the usual defense against post-hoc threshold tuning — someone else checking the reasoning — is unavailable. The S2_Evaluation session on 2026-08-08 surfaced this explicitly (Q25: "who is the sports science reviewer?" — the user confirmed it was himself) and answered it structurally: commit the thresholds and decision records to version control **before the data exists**, so the pre-registration carries a verifiable timestamp instead of an assertion.

## Key Points

- **Asking "who reviews this?" is a design question, not an administrative one.** The answer changes which safeguards are load-bearing; a design that assumes a reviewer and does not have one is unguarded in a way nobody notices.
- **A timestamp in git is falsifiable; a claim in a document is not.** Nine ADRs were committed at 22:46:32, before the CSV export existed, making "these thresholds were fixed in advance" checkable by a third party rather than taken on trust.
- **Pre-commitment must include the negative outcome.** S2 pre-declared that a negative gate result — no athlete clears the 1.5-SD threshold — is still written up and published. Without that rule, a threshold silently becomes a filter for interesting-looking output.
- **Absolute thresholds pre-commit; relative ones do not.** "≥1.5 population SD" can return zero names; "top 3 by deviation" always returns three, so it encodes no prior claim about what counts as unusual and cannot be violated by the data.
- **Record decisions only where trade-offs are real.** ADRs were written for consequential choices and deliberately omitted for cheap-to-reverse presentation questions, keeping the decision log a signal rather than a transcript.

## Details

The mechanism this defends against is not dishonesty but ordinary drift. An analyst who sets a threshold after seeing the data cannot fully separate "this cut point is principled" from "this cut point produces a plausible-looking list of names," and no amount of good faith resolves the ambiguity from the inside. External review normally breaks the loop by introducing a reader who did not see the intermediate results. When that reader does not exist, the loop must be broken temporally instead: the decision is fixed at a point where the data could not have influenced it, and that point is made externally verifiable. Git supplies exactly this — an authenticated ordering of commits that a skeptic can inspect without trusting the author's account of when they decided what.

The distinction between absolute and relative thresholds is what makes the pre-registration bite. A relative rule ("flag the top 3") is unfalsifiable by construction: whatever the data look like, it produces the same quantity of output, so committing to it in advance commits to nothing. An absolute rule ("flag anyone past 1.5 population SD") encodes a substantive prior claim about what magnitude is worth a coach's attention, and it can be wrong — it can return nobody. That possibility is the whole point, which is why the companion rule (publish the negative result) is not an afterthought. A threshold that is only reported when it fires has been quietly converted back into a selection procedure. The same logic explains why the room-size floor came with a *renamed* fallback rather than a silent one: changing the comparison population changes what the number means, so the artifact's claim has to change with it.

The practice generalizes beyond statistics to any output whose quality cannot be checked from the output alone. The recurring theme across this knowledge base — verify at ground truth rather than trusting the layer above — usually applies downstream, to results. Pre-registration is the upstream form: when downstream verification is impossible because there is no independent channel to verify against, move the check earlier, to a point where the reasoning can still be pinned down and time-stamped. The cost is small and front-loaded; the alternative is an analysis whose thresholds are, in principle, unauditable. # Pre-Registration as a Substitute for an Absent External Reviewer

When an analysis has no second reader, the usual defense against post-hoc threshold tuning — someone else checking the reasoning — is unavailable. The S2_Evaluation session on 2026-08-08 surfaced this explicitly (Q25: "who is the sports science reviewer?" — the user confirmed it was himself) and answered it structurally: commit the thresholds and decision records to version control **before the data exists**, so the pre-registration carries a verifiable timestamp instead of an assertion.

## Key Points

- **Asking "who reviews this?" is a design question, not an administrative one.** The answer changes which safeguards are load-bearing; a design that assumes a reviewer and does not have one is unguarded in a way nobody notices.
- **A timestamp in git is falsifiable; a claim in a document is not.** Nine ADRs were committed at 22:46:32, before the CSV export existed, making "these thresholds were fixed in advance" checkable by a third party rather than taken on trust.
- **Pre-commitment must include the negative outcome.** S2 pre-declared that a negative gate result — no athlete clears the 1.5-SD threshold — is still written up and published. Without that rule, a threshold silently becomes a filter for interesting-looking output.
- **Absolute thresholds pre-commit; relative ones do not.** "≥1.5 population SD" can return zero names; "top 3 by deviation" always returns three, so it encodes no prior claim about what counts as unusual and cannot be violated by the data.
- **Record decisions only where trade-offs are real.** ADRs were written for consequential choices and deliberately omitted for cheap-to-reverse presentation questions, keeping the decision log a signal rather than a transcript.

## Details

The mechanism this defends against is not dishonesty but ordinary drift. An analyst who sets a threshold after seeing the data cannot fully separate "this cut point is principled" from "this cut point produces a plausible-looking list of names," and no amount of good faith resolves the ambiguity from the inside. External review normally breaks the loop by introducing a reader who did not see the intermediate results. When that reader does not exist, the loop must be broken temporally instead: the decision is fixed at a point where the data could not have influenced it, and that point is made externally verifiable. Git supplies exactly this — an authenticated ordering of commits that a skeptic can inspect without trusting the author's account of when they decided what.

The distinction between absolute and relative thresholds is what makes the pre-registration bite. A relative rule ("flag the top 3") is unfalsifiable by construction: whatever the data look like, it produces the same quantity of output, so committing to it in advance commits to nothing. An absolute rule ("flag anyone past 1.5 population SD") encodes a substantive prior claim about what magnitude is worth a coach's attention, and it can be wrong — it can return nobody. That possibility is the whole point, which is why the companion rule (publish the negative result) is not an afterthought. A threshold that is only reported when it fires has been quietly converted back into a selection procedure. The same logic explains why the room-size floor came with a *renamed* fallback rather than a silent one: changing the comparison population changes what the number means, so the artifact's claim has to change with it.

The practice generalizes beyond statistics to any output whose quality cannot be checked from the output alone. The recurring theme across this knowledge base — verify at ground truth rather than trusting the layer above — usually applies downstream, to results. Pre-registration is the upstream form: when downstream verification is impossible because there is no independent channel to verify against, move the check earlier, to a point where the reasoning can still be pinned down and time-stamped. The cost is small and front-loaded; the alternative is an analysis whose thresholds are, in principle, unauditable. A related discipline is to keep the record proportional: writing an ADR for every choice dilutes the log until the consequential commitments are indistinguishable from formatting preferences, so only decisions with genuine trade-offs earn a record.

- **Review diversifies in space; pre-registration diversifies in time.** One adds independent readers of a finished thing; the other fixes the decision at a moment when the data could not have influenced it and makes that moment externally checkable.

The multi-stage pattern works on a specific shape of problem: an object exists, it has properties, and different checks are sensitive to different properties. Spec-compliance asks "does this match what was asked for"; code-quality asks "is this correct." Both interrogate the same finished implementation, and their union covers more of it than either alone. The generalizable move is to make the checks *differ in what they are sensitive to*, which is why re-running the first check more carefully would have failed — the blind spot was in the criteria, not the effort.
